screens.title: Account Locking, Password Policies, and Expiration
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we look at the full lifecycle of account security: how passwords age, how complexity gets enforced, and how accounts are locked or expired. You will learn the commands and configuration files you use as an administrator, and the practical trade-offs that affect users and security. We start by defining password aging and how chage and /etc/login. defs work together to set defaults and per-account values. Then we'll review PAM password modules, especially pam_pwquality, and the parameters that control length, character classes, and history. Next, we'll cover account locking strategies: automatic locks after failed logins using pam_faillock, and manual or expiration-based locks using passwd and chage. Finally, we'll examine auditing steps and scripts you can use to report status for compliance. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes — like overly strict complexity or setting very short maximum ages — and show safe testing practices to avoid locking yourself out. By the end you’ll understand both the technical commands and the human impact so you can design balanced, auditable policies.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Account Locking & Policies
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Account Locking, Password Policies, and Expiration

Learn the commands and PAM settings you use to enforce password lifecycle, complexity, and locking while avoiding common pitfalls.

Duration: ~12 minutes
In this lesson
Password aging with chage
Coming up
PAM pwquality configuration
Hands-on
Locking strategies & auditing
Overview timeline
Password lifecycle
Create → Age → Warn → Expire → Inactive/Lock. Use chage for per-user values; use login.defs for new-user defaults. Balance security and usability.
Quick commands
sudo chage -l username
sudo chage -M 90 -m 7 -W 14 username
sudo passwd -l user   # lock
sudo passwd -u user   # unlock
Key Takeaway

Policy is both technical and human. Use chage and PAM to enforce rules, but test in non-production and communicate expiration dates to users to avoid disruptions.

Concept Map
chage • login.defs • pam_pwquality • pam_faillock • passwd
These elements combine to create a system-wide policy and per-user exceptions. Use auditing scripts to verify compliance across accounts.
Why this matters

Weak lifecycle controls or misconfigured PAM can let compromised credentials persist or lock legitimate users out. Balance and testing are essential.

Quick audit tips
  • List aging with chage -l
  • Check login.defs for defaults
  • Search PAM configs for pam_pwquality and pam_faillock

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These first objectives orient practical skills and reasoning you need to manage password lifecycle and account locking. First, you will implement password aging with chage and interpret the fields shown by chage -l so you can set maximum age, minimum days between changes, warning days, inactivity, and absolute expiration. I’ll show how an organization selects sensible defaults and why you must apply chage to existing users while using login. defs for new users. Second, you will configure system-wide password complexity using PAM modules like pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib. You will learn the key parameters—minimum length, credits for digits, upper and lower case, special characters, history, and reject_username—and see why excessive complexity is a hazard rather than a cure. Third, you will automate account locking both for repeated failed logins using pam_faillock and for inactivity or lifecycle end using chage and passwd -l. We’ll examine commands to check and reset faillock counters. Fourth, you will run audits and produce reports: scripted checks across /etc/passwd, grep for PAM lines, and scanning /etc/shadow for locked accounts. Each objective is practical and testable so you can prove policy compliance and avoid accidental lockouts.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: These practical objectives translate policy into repeatable tasks. First, you will update /etc/login. defs safely to set system defaults like PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE, and understand that changes affect newly created users while existing accounts need chage. Second, you will craft and test a pam_pwquality configuration line in the system password stack to require minimum length, digits, upper and lower case, special characters, and a password history. You will practice rejecting username-based passwords and enabling remember to prevent reuse. Third, you will create and manage temporary users with chage -E to schedule expirations and use chage -I to configure inactivity locks after expiry. You will learn how and when to use passwd -l and passwd -u for quick manual locks and unlocks. Fourth, you will run the hands-on audit steps: loop over regular accounts with awk and chage -l, grep PAM files for pam_pwquality and pam_faillock, and scan /etc/shadow for exclamation marks indicating locked passwords. Each task emphasizes safe testing and verification so you never lock out administrators unintentionally.

screens.title: Password Aging and chage Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Password aging enforces that users periodically change passwords and helps limit the window of exposure after credential compromise. The chage utility is the per-user tool that shows and sets these lifecycle parameters. Run chage -l username to see items like last password change, password expiry date, and account expiration. There are key flags to know: -M sets maximum days a password is valid, -m sets the minimum days before change, -W sets warning days to notify users before expiry, -E sets an absolute account expiration date, and -I sets inactivity days after expiry before the account becomes locked. A concrete example is setting a ninety-day maximum with a seven-day minimum and a fourteen-day warning: sudo chage -M 90 -m 7 -W 14 alice. This ensures users keep fresh passwords but cannot immediately cycle back to old passwords if paired with remember in PAM. A common misconception is that changing /etc/login. defs updates existing users; it only affects new accounts. Existing users require chage to change per-account values. Finally, always test changes in a non-production environment and keep a recovery method such as console access or a separate root credential to avoid locking yourself out. How would you verify an account's expiry after making a change? Run chage -l and check the listed expiry and inactivity fields.

keyIdea.title: chage is per-user

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Password Aging
chage flags and meaning
  • -l list aging information for a user.
  • -M maximum days a password is valid.
  • -m minimum days before password change.
  • -W warning days before expiration.
  • -E absolute account expiration date.
  • -I inactivity days after expiry before lock.
Concrete example
sudo chage -M 90 -m 7 -W 14 alice
sudo chage -l alice
Run chage -l to verify the resulting expiry and warning.
Explanation and common misconception
Changing /etc/login.defs affects defaults for newly created accounts only. Administrators often expect it to update existing users, but you must run chage on those accounts. Misconfiguring PASS_MAX_DAYS too low can frustrate users; too high reduces security. Choose values that balance organizational policy and user workflow, and document the change.
Key Takeaway

Use chage for per-user settings and login.defs for defaults. Always verify with chage -l and test policies before broad rollout.

screens.title: System-wide Defaults in /etc/login.defs
screens.narratorSegment: The file /etc/login. defs defines system-wide defaults used when creating new user accounts. Important variables are PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE. PASS_MAX_DAYS defines how long a password remains valid before the user must change it. PASS_MIN_DAYS prevents immediate password changes, which helps enforce a non-trivial password history when combined with PAM's remember setting. PASS_WARN_AGE sets how many days before expiration the system warns users. A practical example: setting PASS_MAX_DAYS to ninety, PASS_MIN_DAYS to seven, and PASS_WARN_AGE to fourteen provides a standard corporate cadence. Remember, changing these values does not retroactively alter current users; those require chage. Administrators commonly forget this and assume new defaults propagate. That misconception leads to gaps between policy and actual account states. When planning a rollout, back up login. defs, communicate the change to users, and update new-user creation workflows. For auditing, grep for PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE to document settings, and then script chage -l for existing users to produce parity reports. Why does this matter? Defaults define the baseline for all future accounts and reduce per-user configuration overhead when set thoughtfully. System-wide Defaults in /etc/login.defs means login.defs sets defaults for newly created accounts; you must use chage to change existing users' aging values.. In practical terms, how defaults apply to new users and what each variable means. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › login.defs Defaults
Key variables in /etc/login.defs
PASS_MAX_DAYS
Maximum password age (days) for new users.
PASS_MIN_DAYS
Minimum days before a password can be changed.
PASS_WARN_AGE
Days of warning before expiry.
Example change sequence: back up the file, edit the three lines to your policy values, and update your user creation scripts so new users receive the intended defaults. Then run audits to compare current users to the new policy.
Audit command
grep -E 'PASS_MAX_DAYS|PASS_MIN_DAYS|PASS_WARN_AGE' /etc/login.defs
Rollout checklist
  • Backup login.defs
  • Update new-user provisioning
  • Run chage -l script for existing users
  • Communicate to users before enforcement

screens.title: Password Complexity with pam_pwquality
screens.narratorSegment: Password complexity is enforced at the point of change by PAM modules like pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib. These modules run in the password stack and check new passwords against configured rules. Important parameters include minlen for minimum length; dcredit, ucredit, lcredit, and ocredit to require digits, uppercase, lowercase, and other characters by using negative values; remember to prevent reuse of recent passwords; reject_username to block passwords derived from the username; and enforce_for_root to apply rules to root. For example, dcredit=-1 requires at least one digit. A practical policy might set minlen to ten, dcredit, ucredit, lcredit, and ocredit to -1 each, and remember=4 to prevent reuse. But beware of a common mistake: making rules too complex leads users to write passwords down or to use predictable patterns, which weakens security. Aim for length and memorability rather than forcing odd substitutions. When you change PAM configuration, test with passwd on a non-critical account to see practical feedback from the module. Finally, remember that pam_pwquality enforces checks on password change only; it does not retroactively update existing passwords. Combining chage and pam_pwquality ensures both lifecycle and complexity are enforced together.

keyIdea.title: PAM enforces quality during change
keyIdea.text: pam_pwquality parameters control length, character classes, history, and username rejection and must be tested to avoid unusable policies.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › pam_pwquality Parameters
Common pam_pwquality options
  • minlen=<N> — set minimum password length.
  • dcredit=<-N> — require digits when negative (dcredit=-1 → one digit).
  • ucredit, lcredit, ocredit — uppercase, lowercase, other characters.
  • remember=<N> — remember last N passwords to prevent reuse.
  • reject_username — prevent username-based passwords.
  • enforce_for_root — apply checks to root as well.
Policy example
password requisite pam_pwquality.so try_first_pass local_users_only retry=3 minlen=10 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 remember=4 reject_username
Place this in the password stack of system-auth or common-password and test carefully.
Practical guidance
  • Favor longer passwords and password history over forcing obscure substitutions.
  • Test policy on new_user to observe prompts and rejections.
  • Document the policy and communicate to users so they can prepare strong, memorable passwords.

screens.title: Example PAM Password Line and Safe Testing
screens.narratorSegment: When editing PAM, you operate in a sensitive authentication stack. The password section usually contains a line for pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib. A representative configuration line enforces length, character credits, retry behavior, and history. For safe changes, back up the PAM file first, then edit and test using a non-privileged test account like new_user. A safe edit sequence is: copy the original file to a. bak, modify the line to include minlen and the credit flags, then attempt passwd new_user to see how the module rejects weak attempts. Here is a typical line for demonstration: password requisite pam_pwquality. so try_first_pass local_users_only retry=3 minlen=10 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 remember=4 reject_username. After you save, run passwd new_user and try weak and strong passwords to observe feedback. If the system becomes unusable or locks you out, use console access or an alternate root shell to revert the. bak. A common misconception is that PAM changes are harmless; in reality a malformed line can block password changes or login. Always keep a recovery path and test incrementally. Example PAM Password Line and Safe Testing means always back up pam files before editing and test changes using a non-critical account to observe real module responses.. In practical terms, edit the password stack and test on a non-production user. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › PAM Example & Test
Recommended edit workflow
  1. Backup file: sudo cp /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/system-auth.bak
  2. Edit carefully and save changes.
  3. Test with a non-critical account: sudo passwd new_user
  4. Revert if unexpected behavior occurs.
Example PAM line
password    requisite     pam_pwquality.so try_first_pass local_users_only retry=3 minlen=10 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 remember=4 reject_username
Place in the password stack of system-auth or common-password depending on your distro.
Testing checklist
  • Try weak passwords and confirm rejection messages.
  • Try a compliant strong password and confirm acceptance.
  • Record the behavior and revert if system login is impaired.

screens.title: Account Locking for Failed Login Attempts
screens.narratorSegment: Preventing brute-force attacks is a core purpose for account locking on repeated failed logins. pam_faillock or older pam_tally2 track authentication failures and can lock accounts after a configured number of denied attempts. Configure pam_faillock in the auth and account stacks, set deny to a threshold such as five, and set an unlock_time to make locks temporary. Administrators can use the faillock command to inspect and reset lock state: faillock --user username shows the counter, and faillock --user username --reset clears it. A concrete policy might deny five attempts and set unlock_time to 900 seconds for automated recovery while logging events for review. A common misconception is that failure counters persist forever; depending on configuration counters may expire after a time, so you must decide whether counters should reset after a period. When testing, trigger failures on a test account to confirm counting and locking behavior, then reset with faillock --reset. Ensure emergency access is available if you misconfigure faillock, because locking an administrative account without a fallback can create an outage. Finally, include lock events in audits so you can detect attack patterns and account misuse.

keyIdea.text: Use pam_faillock to deny repeated failures with a temporary unlock_time and use faillock commands to inspect and reset counters responsibly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Failed Login Locking
Configure pam_faillock
Add pam_faillock entries to the auth and account stacks. Example parameters include deny=5 and unlock_time=900. Decide whether to persist counters across reboots and how long counters age out.
faillock commands
sudo faillock --user alice   # check status
sudo faillock --user alice --reset  # reset counter
Test on a non-critical account by intentionally failing authentication until counter increments and the account locks. Then run the reset command to clear the counter. Log events and include them in your audit feed so you can detect repeated attacks against accounts.
Misconception
Assuming locks are permanent. Configure unlock_time and counter expiration to avoid indefinite denial of service for legitimate users.
Pro Tip

Log faillock events centrally and combine with other signals before taking user-focused actions to distinguish attack from mistake.

screens.title: Manual and Inactivity-based Account Locking
screens.narratorSegment: Not all account locks come from failed logins. Administrators often need to immediately disable an account or schedule its expiration. Manually locking a password with passwd -l username prepends an exclamation mark to the password hash in /etc/shadow, making password-based authentication impossible while preserving the account and home directory. Unlocking uses passwd -u username. For scheduled expiration, chage -E YYYY-MM-DD sets an absolute date after which the account is locked automatically. Additionally, chage -I configures how many days after password expiry the account becomes inactive and unusable. These tools are useful for temporary contractors, alumni, or dormant accounts. The hands-on example in the chapter creates temp_user and sets a six-month expiration with chage -E. A key operational point is that passwd -l is reversible and quick, but lacks a clear expiration date in auditing outputs; chage -E provides a clear, auditable expiration date. For inactive accounts, script use of lastlog or chage -l to identify dormancy and then apply passwd -l or chage -E depending on your policy. When you lock accounts, record the action and reason so reactivation can be handled with proper review.

narration.text: Not all account locks come from failed logins. Administrators often need to immediately disable an account or schedule its expiration. Manually locking a password with passwd -l username prepends an exclamation mark to the password hash in /etc/shadow, making password-based authentication impossible while preserving the account and home directory. Unlocking uses passwd -u username. For scheduled expiration, chage -E YYYY-MM-DD sets an absolute date after which the account is locked automatically. Additionally, chage -I configures how many days after password expiry the account becomes inactive and unusable. These tools are useful for temporary contractors, alumni, or dormant accounts. The hands-on example in the chapter creates temp_user and sets a six-month expiration with chage -E. A key operational point is that passwd -l is reversible and quick, but lacks a clear expiration date in auditing outputs; chage -E provides a clear, auditable expiration date. For inactive accounts, script use of lastlog or chage -l to identify dormancy and then apply passwd -l or chage -E depending on your policy. When you lock accounts, record the action and reason so reactivation can be handled with proper review.

keyIdea.title: Two locking styles
keyIdea.text: Use passwd -l for immediate manual locks and chage -E/-I for scheduled expirations and inactivity-based automation with clearer audit trails.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Manual & Inactivity Locks
Manual lock: passwd -l / -u
sudo passwd -l testuser   # lock
sudo passwd -u testuser   # unlock
passwd -l sets a '!' in /etc/shadow and is quick to apply and revert. It is ideal for immediate suspensions when you want to avoid deletion.
Scheduled expiration: chage -E / inactivity -I
sudo chage -E 2025-01-01 temp_user
sudo chage -I 30 john_doe
chage -E sets an auditable expiration date; chage -I controls how many days after expiry the account becomes inactive.
Dormant account strategy
  • Detect inactivity with lastlog or chage -l reports.
  • Decide between immediate lock or scheduled expiry based on business needs.
  • Record lock rationale and reactivation process for audits.

screens.title: Auditing and Reporting Account Status
screens.narratorSegment: Auditing account and password state is a repeatable administrative task. Use chage -l to inspect a single user, and combine it with awk to loop over regular accounts. The chapter provides a useful script pattern: iterate over /etc/passwd for UIDs greater than or equal to 1000 and run chage -l for each account, producing human-readable sections. Use grep against /etc/login. defs to capture system defaults for PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE. To verify password complexity enforcement, grep for pam_pwquality in PAM files; to verify failed-login protections, grep for pam_faillock. To find manually locked accounts, examine /etc/shadow for lines containing an exclamation mark, which indicates passwd -l has been used. Combine these checks into a report that lists accounts with expired passwords, accounts locked by faillock, and accounts manually locked. A practical example in the chapter shows how to detect expired passwords by comparing expiry dates from chage -l against the current date. When auditing, prioritize readability: include username, last change, expiry, inactivity, and lock status so reviewers can act. Regular automated reports help detect drift between policy and actual account settings.

keyIdea.title: Make audits actionable
keyIdea.text: Script chage -l across regular users, grep login.defs and PAM files, and scan /etc/shadow to produce a clear, auditable report of account state.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Auditing & Reporting
Script pattern for chage across users
for u in $(awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 && $1 != "nfsnobody" {print $1}' /etc/passwd); do
  echo "--- $u ---"
  chage -l $u
done
This lists aging info for regular users for review or to feed into reports.
Useful greps
  • grep -E 'PASS_MAX_DAYS|PASS_MIN_DAYS|PASS_WARN_AGE' /etc/login.defs
  • grep pam_pwquality /etc/pam.d/*
  • grep pam_faillock /etc/pam.d/*
Detect locked accounts
cat /etc/shadow | grep '!'
# Shows accounts with an exclamation mark indicating passwd -l
Combine these outputs into a CSV or human-friendly report and schedule it regularly to detect drift from policy.

screens.title: Hands-on: Implement a Comprehensive Policy
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on workflow implements a comprehensive policy end-to-end. Step one: update system-wide defaults in /etc/login. defs to your chosen values, for example PASS_MAX_DAYS 90, PASS_MIN_DAYS 7, PASS_WARN_AGE 14, after backing up the file. Step two: edit your PAM password stack and add or tune pam_pwquality options to require minimum length, digits, mixed case, special characters, and remember the last four passwords. Back up any PAM files before editing. Step three: create a temporary user and set an absolute expiration six months from now using chage -E and verify with chage -l. Step four: configure inactivity handling for a sample user with chage -I 30 so the account becomes inactive thirty days after password expiry. Step five: simulate locks with passwd -l on a test account and unlock it with passwd -u to practice recovery. Step six: test failed-login protections by configuring pam_faillock deny and unlock_time, then trigger failures and reset counters with faillock --reset. Step seven: run the audit scripts to list aging and locked accounts and confirm compliance. At every step, test on non-critical accounts, record your changes, and keep a console recovery option available.

keyIdea.title: Stepwise rollout
keyIdea.text: Follow a predictable sequence: backup, change defaults, tune PAM, create and test users, configure locks, and audit. Always test first.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Hands-on Workflow
Implementation steps
  1. Backup /etc/login.defs and set PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE.
  2. Backup PAM files and add pam_pwquality options in the password stack.
  3. Create temp_user and set chage -E to six months from today; verify with chage -l.
  4. Set inactivity with chage -I 30 for sample accounts.
  5. Configure pam_faillock deny and unlock_time; test with failures and faillock --reset.
  6. Use passwd -l and passwd -u for manual lock/unlock practice.
  7. Run audit scripts to list aging, locks, and PAM settings for a final report.
Caution

Always maintain console/root recovery before changing PAM or lock settings to avoid accidental lockouts.

Verify

Confirm with chage -l, faillock --user, and grep checks, and document results for compliance records.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Balanced Policy Design
screens.narratorSegment: Designing password and locking policies involves trade-offs. Two common mistakes are making password rules too strict and applying one-size-fits-all settings without considering account roles. Overly strict complexity — many required character classes and short expiry intervals — often produces insecure workarounds: users write passwords down or reuse patterns. Conversely, lax policies with very long PASS_MAX_DAYS increase the attack window if credentials are compromised. A balanced approach uses longer minimum lengths and memory-based history to encourage passphrases rather than forcing obtuse substitutions. For locking, harsh permanent locks without a timed unlock_time can create denial of service for legitimate users or admins. Prefer temporary locks with a reasonable unlock_time combined with logging and review. Another useful pattern is role-based differentiation: apply stricter controls and shorter expiry for privileged accounts while using moderate defaults for general users. Always include testing, backups, and a communication plan when you change policies. In audits, look for drift where user settings diverge from defaults and remediate with chage scripts. The central question is: does the policy reduce risk without creating operational shortcuts that weaken security? If not, iterate until it does.

keyIdea.title: Balance is essential
keyIdea.text: Avoid extremes: choose policies that reduce risk while remaining usable to prevent insecure workarounds and operational outages.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Mistakes & Design
Too strict
Forcing many specialist characters and very short expiry can push users to write passwords down or reuse patterns. This weakens security despite good intentions.
Avoid: extremely short PASS_MAX_DAYS and excessive credit requirements without guidance.
Too lax
Allowing very long expiry or weak complexity increases the window for compromised credentials to be used. This raises risk, especially for privileged accounts.
Avoid: PASS_MAX_DAYS set very high and no pam_pwquality enforcement.
Balanced patterns
  • Favor longer passphrases and history over arcane complexity rules.
  • Use role-based defaults: tighter for admins, moderate for general users.
  • Set temporary lockouts with logging rather than permanent silencing.

screens.title: Safe Testing and Recovery Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Changing authentication configuration carries operational risk. Before making changes, always back up the original files: copy /etc/pam. d/system-auth or /etc/pam. d/common-password and /etc/login. defs. Make a single, small change, then test using a non-privileged test account to confirm both rejection and acceptance behavior. Keep a recovery path: console access, an unlocked root shell, or an out-of-band administrative method so you can revert a bad change. If your distribution supports it, use a separate admin account exempt from strict new policies while testing. When deploying changes broadly, stage them: test environment, small pilot group, then global rollout. Document each change in a change log with rationale and rollback steps. For accidental lockouts, revert the backup, or use passwd -u to unlock specific accounts if necessary, and use faillock --reset to clear failure counters after remedial action. Finally, schedule audit runs after changes to confirm the system is enforcing policies as intended and to detect any unexpected locked accounts or expired passwords. These precautions prevent outages and ensure safe, auditable policy changes. Safe Testing and Recovery Best Practices means always back up configs, test on non-critical accounts, maintain console access, and stage rollouts to avoid accidental lockouts.. In practical terms, minimize risk when changing pam or global defaults. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Testing & Recovery
Backup and rollback
Always copy original files before editing, for example sudo cp /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/system-auth.bak. Keep rollback steps documented including how to restore files and which services to restart if needed.
Staged testing
  • Test locally on non-critical accounts.
  • Pilot with a small user group.
  • Roll out system-wide after verification.
Emergency recovery

Keep console or alternate root access and test reverting backups. Use passwd -u and faillock --reset to repair specific account issues while you restore configurations.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Summarizing the chapter, remember three core concepts. First, chage and /etc/login. defs together shape password lifecycle: chage controls per-user settings while login. defs sets defaults for new accounts. Second, pam_pwquality (or pam_cracklib) enforces complexity at password change; tune minlen, credit flags, remember, and reject_username while avoiding overly strict rules that encourage insecure workarounds. Third, account locking has two forms: automatic locks after failed attempts with pam_faillock and manual or scheduled locks using passwd -l and chage -E/-I. Regular auditing—running chage -l across users, grepping PAM configs, and scanning /etc/shadow for locked indicators—turns policy into evidence that you can use for compliance and operational review. Keep backups and test plans before making changes so you can recover if authentication is affected. These three ideas form the operational core of account security in Linux environments.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we look at the full lifecycle of account security: how passwords age, how complexity gets enforced, and how accounts are locked or expired. You will learn the commands and configuration files you use as an administrator, and the practical trade-offs that affect users and security. We start by defining password aging and how chage and /etc/login. defs work together to set defaults and per-account values. Then we'll review PAM password modules, especially pam_pwquality, and the parameters that control length, character classes, and history. Next, we'll cover account locking strategies: automatic locks after failed logins using pam_faillock, and manual or expiration-based locks using passwd and chage. Finally, we'll examine auditing steps and scripts you can use to report status for compliance. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes — like overly strict complexity or setting very short maximum ages — and show safe testing practices to avoid locking yourself out. By the end you’ll understand both the technical commands and the human impact so you can design balanced, auditable policies.

These first objectives orient practical skills and reasoning you need to manage password lifecycle and account locking. First, you will implement password aging with chage and interpret the fields shown by chage -l so you can set maximum age, minimum days between changes, warning days, inactivity, and absolute expiration. I’ll show how an organization selects sensible defaults and why you must apply chage to existing users while using login. defs for new users. Second, you will configure system-wide password complexity using PAM modules like pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib. You will learn the key parameters—minimum length, credits for digits, upper and lower case, special characters, history, and reject_username—and see why excessive complexity is a hazard rather than a cure. Third, you will automate account locking both for repeated failed logins using pam_faillock and for inactivity or lifecycle end using chage and passwd -l. We’ll examine commands to check and reset faillock counters. Fourth, you will run audits and produce reports: scripted checks across /etc/passwd, grep for PAM lines, and scanning /etc/shadow for locked accounts. Each objective is practical and testable so you can prove policy compliance and avoid accidental lockouts.

These practical objectives translate policy into repeatable tasks. First, you will update /etc/login. defs safely to set system defaults like PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE, and understand that changes affect newly created users while existing accounts need chage. Second, you will craft and test a pam_pwquality configuration line in the system password stack to require minimum length, digits, upper and lower case, special characters, and a password history. You will practice rejecting username-based passwords and enabling remember to prevent reuse. Third, you will create and manage temporary users with chage -E to schedule expirations and use chage -I to configure inactivity locks after expiry. You will learn how and when to use passwd -l and passwd -u for quick manual locks and unlocks. Fourth, you will run the hands-on audit steps: loop over regular accounts with awk and chage -l, grep PAM files for pam_pwquality and pam_faillock, and scan /etc/shadow for exclamation marks indicating locked passwords. Each task emphasizes safe testing and verification so you never lock out administrators unintentionally.

Password aging enforces that users periodically change passwords and helps limit the window of exposure after credential compromise. The chage utility is the per-user tool that shows and sets these lifecycle parameters. Run chage -l username to see items like last password change, password expiry date, and account expiration. There are key flags to know: -M sets maximum days a password is valid, -m sets the minimum days before change, -W sets warning days to notify users before expiry, -E sets an absolute account expiration date, and -I sets inactivity days after expiry before the account becomes locked. A concrete example is setting a ninety-day maximum with a seven-day minimum and a fourteen-day warning: sudo chage -M 90 -m 7 -W 14 alice. This ensures users keep fresh passwords but cannot immediately cycle back to old passwords if paired with remember in PAM. A common misconception is that changing /etc/login. defs updates existing users; it only affects new accounts. Existing users require chage to change per-account values. Finally, always test changes in a non-production environment and keep a recovery method such as console access or a separate root credential to avoid locking yourself out. How would you verify an account's expiry after making a change? Run chage -l and check the listed expiry and inactivity fields.

The file /etc/login. defs defines system-wide defaults used when creating new user accounts. Important variables are PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE. PASS_MAX_DAYS defines how long a password remains valid before the user must change it. PASS_MIN_DAYS prevents immediate password changes, which helps enforce a non-trivial password history when combined with PAM's remember setting. PASS_WARN_AGE sets how many days before expiration the system warns users. A practical example: setting PASS_MAX_DAYS to ninety, PASS_MIN_DAYS to seven, and PASS_WARN_AGE to fourteen provides a standard corporate cadence. Remember, changing these values does not retroactively alter current users; those require chage. Administrators commonly forget this and assume new defaults propagate. That misconception leads to gaps between policy and actual account states. When planning a rollout, back up login. defs, communicate the change to users, and update new-user creation workflows. For auditing, grep for PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE to document settings, and then script chage -l for existing users to produce parity reports. Why does this matter? Defaults define the baseline for all future accounts and reduce per-user configuration overhead when set thoughtfully. System-wide Defaults in /etc/login.defs means login.defs sets defaults for newly created accounts; you must use chage to change existing users' aging values.. In practical terms, how defaults apply to new users and what each variable means. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Password complexity is enforced at the point of change by PAM modules like pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib. These modules run in the password stack and check new passwords against configured rules. Important parameters include minlen for minimum length; dcredit, ucredit, lcredit, and ocredit to require digits, uppercase, lowercase, and other characters by using negative values; remember to prevent reuse of recent passwords; reject_username to block passwords derived from the username; and enforce_for_root to apply rules to root. For example, dcredit=-1 requires at least one digit. A practical policy might set minlen to ten, dcredit, ucredit, lcredit, and ocredit to -1 each, and remember=4 to prevent reuse. But beware of a common mistake: making rules too complex leads users to write passwords down or to use predictable patterns, which weakens security. Aim for length and memorability rather than forcing odd substitutions. When you change PAM configuration, test with passwd on a non-critical account to see practical feedback from the module. Finally, remember that pam_pwquality enforces checks on password change only; it does not retroactively update existing passwords. Combining chage and pam_pwquality ensures both lifecycle and complexity are enforced together.

When editing PAM, you operate in a sensitive authentication stack. The password section usually contains a line for pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib. A representative configuration line enforces length, character credits, retry behavior, and history. For safe changes, back up the PAM file first, then edit and test using a non-privileged test account like new_user. A safe edit sequence is: copy the original file to a. bak, modify the line to include minlen and the credit flags, then attempt passwd new_user to see how the module rejects weak attempts. Here is a typical line for demonstration: password requisite pam_pwquality. so try_first_pass local_users_only retry=3 minlen=10 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 remember=4 reject_username. After you save, run passwd new_user and try weak and strong passwords to observe feedback. If the system becomes unusable or locks you out, use console access or an alternate root shell to revert the. bak. A common misconception is that PAM changes are harmless; in reality a malformed line can block password changes or login. Always keep a recovery path and test incrementally. Example PAM Password Line and Safe Testing means always back up pam files before editing and test changes using a non-critical account to observe real module responses.. In practical terms, edit the password stack and test on a non-production user. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Preventing brute-force attacks is a core purpose for account locking on repeated failed logins. pam_faillock or older pam_tally2 track authentication failures and can lock accounts after a configured number of denied attempts. Configure pam_faillock in the auth and account stacks, set deny to a threshold such as five, and set an unlock_time to make locks temporary. Administrators can use the faillock command to inspect and reset lock state: faillock --user username shows the counter, and faillock --user username --reset clears it. A concrete policy might deny five attempts and set unlock_time to 900 seconds for automated recovery while logging events for review. A common misconception is that failure counters persist forever; depending on configuration counters may expire after a time, so you must decide whether counters should reset after a period. When testing, trigger failures on a test account to confirm counting and locking behavior, then reset with faillock --reset. Ensure emergency access is available if you misconfigure faillock, because locking an administrative account without a fallback can create an outage. Finally, include lock events in audits so you can detect attack patterns and account misuse.

Not all account locks come from failed logins. Administrators often need to immediately disable an account or schedule its expiration. Manually locking a password with passwd -l username prepends an exclamation mark to the password hash in /etc/shadow, making password-based authentication impossible while preserving the account and home directory. Unlocking uses passwd -u username. For scheduled expiration, chage -E YYYY-MM-DD sets an absolute date after which the account is locked automatically. Additionally, chage -I configures how many days after password expiry the account becomes inactive and unusable. These tools are useful for temporary contractors, alumni, or dormant accounts. The hands-on example in the chapter creates temp_user and sets a six-month expiration with chage -E. A key operational point is that passwd -l is reversible and quick, but lacks a clear expiration date in auditing outputs; chage -E provides a clear, auditable expiration date. For inactive accounts, script use of lastlog or chage -l to identify dormancy and then apply passwd -l or chage -E depending on your policy. When you lock accounts, record the action and reason so reactivation can be handled with proper review.

Auditing account and password state is a repeatable administrative task. Use chage -l to inspect a single user, and combine it with awk to loop over regular accounts. The chapter provides a useful script pattern: iterate over /etc/passwd for UIDs greater than or equal to 1000 and run chage -l for each account, producing human-readable sections. Use grep against /etc/login. defs to capture system defaults for PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS, and PASS_WARN_AGE. To verify password complexity enforcement, grep for pam_pwquality in PAM files; to verify failed-login protections, grep for pam_faillock. To find manually locked accounts, examine /etc/shadow for lines containing an exclamation mark, which indicates passwd -l has been used. Combine these checks into a report that lists accounts with expired passwords, accounts locked by faillock, and accounts manually locked. A practical example in the chapter shows how to detect expired passwords by comparing expiry dates from chage -l against the current date. When auditing, prioritize readability: include username, last change, expiry, inactivity, and lock status so reviewers can act. Regular automated reports help detect drift between policy and actual account settings.

This hands-on workflow implements a comprehensive policy end-to-end. Step one: update system-wide defaults in /etc/login. defs to your chosen values, for example PASS_MAX_DAYS 90, PASS_MIN_DAYS 7, PASS_WARN_AGE 14, after backing up the file. Step two: edit your PAM password stack and add or tune pam_pwquality options to require minimum length, digits, mixed case, special characters, and remember the last four passwords. Back up any PAM files before editing. Step three: create a temporary user and set an absolute expiration six months from now using chage -E and verify with chage -l. Step four: configure inactivity handling for a sample user with chage -I 30 so the account becomes inactive thirty days after password expiry. Step five: simulate locks with passwd -l on a test account and unlock it with passwd -u to practice recovery. Step six: test failed-login protections by configuring pam_faillock deny and unlock_time, then trigger failures and reset counters with faillock --reset. Step seven: run the audit scripts to list aging and locked accounts and confirm compliance. At every step, test on non-critical accounts, record your changes, and keep a console recovery option available.

Designing password and locking policies involves trade-offs. Two common mistakes are making password rules too strict and applying one-size-fits-all settings without considering account roles. Overly strict complexity — many required character classes and short expiry intervals — often produces insecure workarounds: users write passwords down or reuse patterns. Conversely, lax policies with very long PASS_MAX_DAYS increase the attack window if credentials are compromised. A balanced approach uses longer minimum lengths and memory-based history to encourage passphrases rather than forcing obtuse substitutions. For locking, harsh permanent locks without a timed unlock_time can create denial of service for legitimate users or admins. Prefer temporary locks with a reasonable unlock_time combined with logging and review. Another useful pattern is role-based differentiation: apply stricter controls and shorter expiry for privileged accounts while using moderate defaults for general users. Always include testing, backups, and a communication plan when you change policies. In audits, look for drift where user settings diverge from defaults and remediate with chage scripts. The central question is: does the policy reduce risk without creating operational shortcuts that weaken security? If not, iterate until it does.

Changing authentication configuration carries operational risk. Before making changes, always back up the original files: copy /etc/pam. d/system-auth or /etc/pam. d/common-password and /etc/login. defs. Make a single, small change, then test using a non-privileged test account to confirm both rejection and acceptance behavior. Keep a recovery path: console access, an unlocked root shell, or an out-of-band administrative method so you can revert a bad change. If your distribution supports it, use a separate admin account exempt from strict new policies while testing. When deploying changes broadly, stage them: test environment, small pilot group, then global rollout. Document each change in a change log with rationale and rollback steps. For accidental lockouts, revert the backup, or use passwd -u to unlock specific accounts if necessary, and use faillock --reset to clear failure counters after remedial action. Finally, schedule audit runs after changes to confirm the system is enforcing policies as intended and to detect any unexpected locked accounts or expired passwords. These precautions prevent outages and ensure safe, auditable policy changes. Safe Testing and Recovery Best Practices means always back up configs, test on non-critical accounts, maintain console access, and stage rollouts to avoid accidental lockouts.. Summarizing the chapter, remember three core concepts. First, chage and /etc/login. defs together shape password lifecycle: chage controls per-user settings while login. defs sets defaults for new accounts. Second, pam_pwquality (or pam_cracklib) enforces complexity at password change; tune minlen, credit flags, remember, and reject_username while avoiding overly strict rules that encourage insecure workarounds. Third, account locking has two forms: automatic locks after failed attempts with pam_faillock and manual or scheduled locks using passwd -l and chage -E/-I. Regular auditing—running chage -l across users, grepping PAM configs, and scanning /etc/shadow for locked indicators—turns policy into evidence that you can use for compliance and operational review. Keep backups and test plans before making changes so you can recover if authentication is affected. These three ideas form the operational core of account security in Linux environments.

Finally, keep these commands at hand as quick references. First, chage manages per-user aging: use chage -l to list and chage with -M, -m, -W, -E, and -I to modify settings. Second, pam_pwquality (or pam_cracklib) is configured in PAM files; tune minlen, credit flags like dcredit and ucredit, remember, and reject_username to enforce quality at change time. Third, account locking utilities include pam_faillock for failed-login protections and the faillock command to inspect and reset counters, plus passwd -l and passwd -u for manual locking and unlocking. For audits, grep the PAM configs and /etc/login. defs and scan /etc/shadow for exclamation marks indicating password locks. Keep a testing plan and backups before changing these components. These commands and files are your operational toolkit for enforcing and verifying account security across systems.
